He was so astonished that for a long while he entertained no notions of danger to himself, his apprehensions being buried in thoughts of "inhuman, hellish brutality."

The evidence also shows that he did not attack them right away because he later reconsidered any plan to do so. In the same chapter, he records that he "began by little and little to be off my design" and concluded that he had "taken wrong measures in my resolution to attack the savages," deciding it was not his business to meddle with them unless they first attacked him. The evidence does not specify exactly how much time passed between his first discovery and this reconsideration, nor does it describe any immediate physical action he took toward the cannibals beyond retreating to his habitation.

attempts.question: Why did Phileas Fogg think he had lost the wager after reaching London, and how did he discover that he had actually won?
attempts.answer:
Phileas Fogg thought he had lost the wager because, on reaching London, he believed he was five minutes behind schedule — the evidence states: "Having made the tour of the world, he was behind-hand five minutes. He had lost the wager!" [Around the World in Eighty Days — Jules Verne, CHAPTER XXXIV.]

He discovered he had actually won because he had gained a day without realizing it. The evidence explains: "Phileas Fogg had, without suspecting it, gained one day on his journey, and this merely because he had travelled constantly _eastward;_ he would, on the contrary, have lost a day had he gone in the opposite direction, that is, _westward_." [Around the World in Eighty Days — Jules Verne, CHAPTER XXXVII.] Specifically, "while Phileas Fogg, going eastward, saw the sun pass the meridian _eighty_ times, his friends in London only saw it pass the meridian _seventy-nine_ times." [Around the World in Eighty Days — Jules Verne, CHAPTER XXXVII.]

The error was corrected when his servant's proposed marriage led to a visit to the Reverend Samuel Wilson, which apprised him of the mistake: "If you had not suggested our marriage, my servant would not have gone to the Reverend Samuel Wilson’s, I should not have been apprised of my error, and—" [Around the World in Eighty Days — Jules Verne, CHAPTER XXXVII.] The evidence also notes the exact correction: "You have made a mistake of one day! We arrived twenty-four hours ahead of time; but there are only ten minutes left!" [Around the World in Eighty Days — Jules Verne, CHAPTER XXXVII.]

The evidence does not specify the exact moment or person who first told Fogg of the date error beyond the marriage-related visit, but it confirms the cause and the correction.

attempts.question: There are two books in my library about knights and chivalry. One seems to take the whole code of honour seriously and the other makes fun of it. Which is which, and how does each one treat the idea of being a knight?
attempts.answer:
The book that takes the code of honour seriously is *Ivanhoe* by Walter Scott, and the book that makes fun of it is *Don Quixote* by Miguel de Cervantes.

In *Ivanhoe*, the knightly code is presented as noble and binding. A character declares, "Such, maiden, are the laws of chivalry to which we are sworn, and to which we offer all that we hold dear" [Ivanhoe — Walter Scott, CHAPTER XXIX]. The same chapter praises chivalry as "the pure light of chivalry, which alone distinguishes the noble from the base, the gentle knight from the churl and the savage; which rates our life far, far beneath the pitch of our honour; raises us victorious over pain, toil, and suffering, and teaches us to fear no evil but disgrace" [Ivanhoe — Walter Scott, CHAPTER XXIX]. However, the book also includes a critical voice: Rebecca questions whether this is "an offering of sacrifice to a demon of vain glory, and a passing through the fire to Moloch" [Ivanhoe — Walter Scott, CHAPTER XXIX], and asks whether "the rusted mail which hangs as a hatchment over the champion's dim and mouldering tomb" and "the defaced sculpture of the inscription" are "sufficient rewards for the sacrifice of every kindly affection, for a life spent miserably that ye may make others miserable" [Ivanhoe — Walter Scott, CHAPTER XXIX]. So while the book treats the ideal seriously, it also dramatizes a challenge to it.

In *Don Quixote*, the treatment is satirical. The novel is described as a "Satire of chivalric romance — the novel parodies the popular romance literature that drove Quixote to madness" [Don Quixote — Miguel de Cervantes, Themes]. A character says, "I shall not be so mad as to make a knight-errant of myself; for I see well enough that things are not now as they used to be in those days, when they say those famous knights roamed about the world" [Don Quixote — Miguel de Cervantes, CHAPTER XXXII.]. Yet the protagonist insists on the honour of the calling: "How little thou knowest about chivalry, Sancho," replied Don Quixote; "hold thy peace and have patience; the day will come when thou shalt see with thine own eyes what an honourable thing it is to wander in the pursuit of this calling" [Don Quixote — Miguel de Cervantes, CHAPTER XVIII.]. The evidence shows the mockery of chivalric ideals, but it does not provide a full account of how the book treats every aspect of being a knight — for instance, it does not cover Quixote's specific adventures or his failures in detail.
